p.src: Now Sun the Great Sage and his two brothers descended from the clouds. They went straight into the court, where the sovereign, his ministers, the heir apparent, and the queen came forward in several ranks to bow in welcome and offer thanks. Pilgrim related to the sovereign and his ministers how the Bodhisattva had subdued the demon and taken the monster away, and they all bowed again and again. While all were offering their congratulations, a chamberlain was heard announcing, “Your Majesty, four more monks have arrived outside.” Eight Rules panicked. “Brother,” he said, “could the monster have worked some magic, counterfeited the Bodhisattva Manjusri to deceive us, and now changed into monks to match wits with us?” Pilgrim said, “How could that possibly be?” He immediately ordered that they be admitted so he could see them.

p.src: The civil and military officials passed down the order to let them enter. When Pilgrim looked, he saw that they were the monks of Baolin Monastery, carrying the sky-soaring crown, the jasper belt, the ocher-yellow robe, and the carefree shoes. Pilgrim was delighted. “Excellent timing! Excellent timing!” he said. He first had the Daoist come forward, remove his headcloth, and put on the sky-soaring crown; take off his cloth gown and don the ocher-yellow robe; untie his cord and fasten the jasper belt; slip off his monk's shoes and step into the carefree shoes; then he told the crown prince to bring out the white jade tablet and place it in his hand, and at once invited him to ascend the throne and proclaim himself sovereign. As the old saying goes, “The court cannot be without a sovereign for a single day.” But the emperor refused to sit on the throne. Weeping, he knelt in the middle of the steps and said, “I have been dead for three years, and now, through the masters' kindness, I have been restored to life. How could I dare presumptuously call myself sovereign again? Let one of the masters become sovereign. I shall gladly take my wife and children outside the city and live as a commoner; that will suffice.” Tripitaka would never accept; his sole desire was to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. They next invited Pilgrim, who laughed and said, “To tell you all the truth, if old Monkey had wanted to be an emperor, he would already have reigned as emperor over every realm and province under Heaven. But we are accustomed to being monks and living free and easy. If I became emperor, I would have to grow out my hair, stay awake after dusk, and get no sleep at the fifth watch. At news from the frontier, my mind would know no peace; at the sight of famine or disaster, I would be helpless with worry. How could we ever grow accustomed to that? You remain your emperor, and I shall remain my monk and go on cultivating merit.” Unable to overcome their earnest refusals, the king had no choice but to ascend the precious throne, face south, and proclaim himself sovereign. He granted a general amnesty throughout the realm, bestowed honors and gifts on the monks of Baolin Monastery, and sent them home. Only then did he open the eastern hall and hold a banquet for the Tang Monk. At the same time, he issued a decree summoning court painters to make joyful portraits of the Tang master and his four disciples, which were enshrined in the Golden Throne Hall.

p.src: Having restored peace to the kingdom, the master and disciples refused to linger and wished to take leave of the royal presence and journey west. The emperor, the consorts and queen of the three palaces, the crown prince, and all the ministers offered the master the kingdom's precious treasures, gold, silver, satin, and silk in gratitude for his kindness. Tripitaka would not accept the smallest portion. He merely had his travel document exchanged and urged Wukong and the others to load the horse and set out at once. The king felt deeply obliged. He arrayed the full imperial carriage, invited the Tang Monk to take the honored seat, and ordered two ranks of civil and military officials to lead the way. He himself, together with the consorts, queen, and crown prince, supported the hub and pushed the wheel, escorting him beyond the city walls. Only then did he descend from the dragon carriage and bid everyone farewell. The king said, “Master, when you return from the Western Heaven with the scriptures, you must be sure to visit my realm once more.” Tripitaka said, “This disciple accepts your command.” The emperor held back the tears brimming in his eyes and then returned with his ministers.

More than half a month passed when suddenly they saw another lofty mountain, truly scraping the heavens and blocking the sun. Tripitaka was alarmed in the saddle. He quickly reined in his horse and urgently called for Pilgrim. Pilgrim said, “What are your instructions, Master?” Tripitaka said, “Look, there are more great mountains and steep ridges ahead. We must be exceedingly vigilant, lest some evil creature suddenly come to attack me again.” Pilgrim laughed. “Just keep traveling and do not worry needlessly again. Old Monkey will protect you.” The elder had no choice but to set his mind at ease. He whipped his horse onward until they reached the mountain cliffs, which proved exceedingly rugged and steep. p.src: Just as the master and disciples were filled with dread, they saw a red cloud rise from a hollow in the mountain, shooting straight into the ninth heaven and gathering into a mass of fiery vapor. Pilgrim was greatly alarmed. He rushed forward, seized the Tang Monk by the foot, and shoved him off the horse, crying, “Brothers, go no farther! A monster is coming!” In the commotion, Eight Rules hastily drew his rake and Sha Monk swiftly brandished his precious staff, surrounding the Tang Monk and guarding him in their midst.

p.src: The story now divides into two. As it turned out, there truly was a monster within the red radiance. Several years earlier, he had heard people say that the Tang Monk from the Eastern Land was journeying to the Western Heaven to obtain the scriptures; that he was the reincarnation of Elder Golden Cicada, a good man cultivated through ten lifetimes; and that whoever ate one piece of his flesh would prolong his life, enjoy longevity, and endure as long as Heaven and Earth. Every day he had waited among the mountains, never expecting the monk to arrive today. As he watched from midair, he saw the three disciples surrounding and guarding the Tang Monk on his horse, each one prepared for battle. The spirit could not praise him enough. “What a fine monk! I just saw a plump, fair-faced monk riding a horse, surely the holy monk of the Tang court. But how has he come to be protected by three ugly monks? Each has bared his fists, drawn up his sleeves, and grasped a weapon, as though ready to fight someone. Ah! I wonder which of them has the keen eye; one of them must have recognized me. With things as they are, I can forget about eating the Tang Monk's flesh.” He pondered for a long while, consulting his own heart. “If I rely on force to capture him, I shall never get near him; but perhaps if I deceive him with an appearance of goodness, I can succeed. If only I can bewilder his mind, I shall devise a scheme within that show of goodness and certainly capture him. I shall go down and toy with him awhile.”

p.src: What a monster! He immediately dispersed the red radiance, lowered his cloud, and descended. He went to the mountainside, shook himself, and changed into a mischievous seven-year-old boy. Stark naked, without a stitch of clothing, he bound his own hands and feet with hempen rope, hung himself high from the crown of a pine tree, and cried again and again, “Help! Help!”

p.src: Now when Sun the Great Sage raised his head and looked again, he saw that the red cloud had completely dispersed and the fiery vapor had entirely vanished. He called, “Master, please mount your horse and let us be on our way.” The Tang Monk said, “You said a monster was coming. How can we dare travel on now?” Pilgrim said, “Just now I saw a red cloud rise from the ground and gather into a mass of fiery vapor in the sky. It was unquestionably a monster. But now the red cloud has dispersed. I imagine it was merely a passing monster with no intention of harming anyone. Let us go.” Eight Rules laughed. “Elder Brother certainly has a clever way with words! Since when are there passing monsters?” Pilgrim said, “What would you know about it? Suppose the demon king of some mountain or cave holds a banquet and invites the spirits from all the surrounding mountains and caves to attend. Then spirits from all four directions—east, west, south, and north—will come to the gathering. Thus their minds are set only on attending the gathering, and they have no intention of harming anyone. That is what I mean by a passing monster.”

p.src: Hearing this, Tripitaka half believed and half doubted him, but could only mount his horse and follow the road toward the mountain. As they went, they suddenly heard a cry: “Help!” The elder was greatly startled and said, “Disciple, who can that be calling out here halfway up the mountain?” Pilgrim stepped forward and said, “Master, just keep going. Never mind about sedan chairs for people, mule litters, open chairs, or sleeping chairs. Even if there were a chair in a place like this, there would be no one to carry you.” The Tang Monk said, “I did not mean a jiào that is carried. I meant the jiào of someone calling out.” Pilgrim laughed and said, “I know. Pay no heed to other people’s business; let us keep going.”

p.src: Tripitaka took his advice, urged his horse on, and continued forward. Before they had gone even a mile, they again heard a cry: “Help!” The elder said, “Disciple, that cry does not come from a ghost or evil spirit. Were it a ghost or evil spirit, it would make a sound but cast no echo. Listen—he calls once and then calls again. It must be someone in distress. We should go and rescue him.” Pilgrim said, “Master, put away that compassionate heart of yours for today. Once we are across this mountain, you may show compassion again. In this place, ill fortune is far more likely than good. You know the saying about spirits inhabiting grasses and trees: any living thing may become a demon. Most kinds are still manageable, but there is one kind of python which, after cultivating itself for many long years and becoming a demon, learns how to call people by their childhood names. If it lies hidden in a clump of grass or a hollow in the hills and calls to someone, all is well so long as the person does not answer; but if he answers even once, it snatches away his primal spirit, follows him that very night, and will surely take his life. Let us go, let us go. The ancients said, ‘Once safely away, give thanks to the gods.’ You must not listen to it.” The elder had no choice but to heed him, and once more whipped his horse onward.

p.src: Pilgrim thought to himself, “I do not know where that wretched fiend is, but it keeps on yelling. Let old Monkey give it the ‘Mao-and-You Star Art’ and make sure the two sides never meet.” Our fine Great Sage called Friar Sand over and said, “Keep close to the horse and walk slowly. Let old Monkey go relieve himself.” He let the Tang Monk go a few paces ahead, then recited a spell and employed the art of moving mountains and shrinking the earth. Pointing his gold-banded staff behind them, he carried master and disciples over the peak and onward, leaving the monster behind.

p.src: He lengthened his stride again, caught up with the Tang Monk, and continued with them through the mountain. Then Tripitaka once more heard a cry from behind the mountain: “Help!” The elder said, “Disciple, that unfortunate person truly lacks good fortune. He never had the chance to meet us, and we have already passed him by. Listen, he is calling from behind the mountain.” Bajie said, “He is actually still in front of the mountain; it is only that the wind has shifted.” Pilgrim said, “Who cares whether the wind has shifted or not? Just keep going.” At that they all fell silent, wishing they could cross the mountain in a single stride. Of this, no more need be said.

p.src: Now the demon on the mountainside called out three or four times in succession, but still no one came. He thought to himself, “I have been waiting for the Tang Monk here. When I saw him, he was less than three miles away, so why has he still not arrived after all this time? They must have taken a shortcut down another road.” He shook his body, slipped free of the ropes, and once more soared into the sky in a streak of red light to look around. Great Sage Sun happened to look back with his face raised. Recognizing the demon, he grabbed the Tang Monk by the feet, shoved him from the horse, and cried, “Brothers, take care! Take care! That demon is coming again!” In alarm, Bajie and Friar Sand each took up rake and staff and once more enclosed the Tang Monk protectively between them.

Otherwise, all my scheming will win no quarry, and all my effort and eagerness will come to nothing.” He lowered his cloud once more and, transforming himself as before, hung high from the top of a pine tree to wait. This time he was less than half a mile away.

p.src: Now Great Sage Sun looked up again. Seeing the red cloud disperse once more, he invited his master to remount and continue. Tripitaka said, “You said the demon was coming again. Why are you now asking me to continue?” Pilgrim said, “It was only a passing demon. It did not dare provoke us.” The elder grew angry again and said, “That wretched monkey makes a complete fool of me. When we truly come to a place inhabited by demons, you say nothing is wrong; yet in a peaceful place like this, you frighten me by continually shouting that some demon or other is here. Most of what you say is false and little of it true. With no regard for gentleness or force, you seized me by the feet and flung me from the horse, yet now you explain it away as a passing demon. Suppose you had injured me in the fall—you would surely have been sorry then! And so on and so forth...” Pilgrim said, “Master, do not blame me. If your hands or feet were hurt in a fall, they could still be treated; but if a demon carried you off, where could we ever hope to find you?” Tripitaka flew into a rage and, grunting with anger, made ready to recite the Tight-Fillet Spell. Only after Friar Sand earnestly dissuaded him did he remount and continue.

p.src: Before he was even firmly seated, they heard another cry: “Master, save me!” The elder raised his head and saw that it was a little child, stark naked and hanging from a tree. He reined in his horse and cursed Pilgrim: “What an utterly lazy and wicked monkey you are! You have not the least good will in you; all you ever think of is behaving outrageously and committing violence! When I told you that the cry was a human voice, you poured out a thousand arguments, insisting it was a demon. Look—is that not a human being hanging from the tree?” Seeing that his master blamed him and confronted by the child’s apparent form, the Great Sage could neither make a move against it nor risk having the Tight-Fillet Spell recited. He lowered his head, dared not answer another word, and let the Tang Monk approach the tree. The elder pointed with the tip of his whip and asked, “Whose child are you? What happened that you came to be hanging here? Tell me, so that I may save you.” Alas! It was plainly a spirit that had transformed itself into such a shape, but the master possessed only mortal eyes and flesh and could not recognize it.

p.src: Seeing him ask questions, the demon put on an even greater show of deceit. With tears in his eyes, he cried, “Master, west of this mountain lies a ravine called Withered Pine Ravine. Beyond it is a village, and that is my home. My great-grandfather’s surname was Hong. Because he amassed such stores of gold and silver and possessed a vast fortune, he was nicknamed Hong the Millionaire. He died of old age long ago, leaving the family property to my father. Of late, extravagant living gradually consumed our fortune, and my father’s nickname became Hong the Hundred-Thousandaire. He made a particular habit of befriending bold men from every quarter and lending out his gold and silver in hopes of earning interest. But how could he know those lawless men would swindle it away? Neither principal nor interest ever returned. My father swore a mighty oath never to lend another penny. Those borrowers, impoverished and at their wits’ end, formed a murderous band. Brandishing torches and weapons, they attacked our house in broad daylight and plundered all our wealth. They killed my father. Finding my mother somewhat attractive, they carried her off to be their bandit chief’s wife. At that time my mother could not bear to leave me. She held me in her arms, weeping bitterly and trembling as she followed the bandits. Unexpectedly, when we reached this mountain, they wanted to kill me too. Only my mother’s desperate pleas saved me from dying beneath their blades. Instead, they hung me from this tree with a rope, meaning for me to freeze and starve to death. Those bandits carried my mother off somewhere, though I know not where. I have hung here for three days and three nights, and not a single traveler has passed. I know not what merit I accumulated in some former life to meet you, venerable master, in this one. If you will show great compassion, save my life, and take me home, I shall sell myself into bondage and devote my life to repaying your kindness. Even when yellow earth covers my face, I shall never dare forget it.”

p.src: When Tripitaka heard this, he took the tale for truth and told Bajie to untie the rope and rescue the child. The fool was no judge of character and was about to step forward and do it. Unable to restrain himself, Pilgrim shouted from beside him, “You wretch! There is someone here who knows what you are. Stop spinning empty tricks and telling lies to deceive people. If your family fortune was plundered, your father slain by bandits, and your mother abducted, to whom are we supposed to deliver you after rescuing you? And what could you give us in thanks? Your lie has fallen apart.” Hearing this, the monster grew afraid. He realized that the Great Sage was a formidable fellow and secretly marked him down in his mind. Then, trembling again and shedding tears, he said, “Master, though both my parents are gone and all our movable wealth is lost, some fields and property remain untouched, and my relatives are all still living.” Pilgrim said, “What relatives do you have?” The monster replied, “My maternal grandfather’s family lives south of the mountain, my father’s sister lives north of the ridge, Li Si at the head of the ravine is my mother’s sister’s husband, and Hong San in the woods is a senior kinsman of my clan. I also have uncles and older cousins living in and around our village. If the venerable master will save me, then when we reach the village and meet all my kin, I shall tell everyone, one by one, of your kindness in rescuing me. We will sell some of the fields and reward you handsomely.”

p.src: Hearing this, Bajie blocked Pilgrim and said, “Brother, why do you keep interrogating a little child like this? He said the bandits merely robbed his movable wealth. Surely they could not have carried off the houses and fields as well? Once he tells his relatives, even with our enormous appetites, we could never eat through the value of ten mu of his land. Let us get him down.” The fool thought only of food and cared nothing for whether the child was good or evil. Using his monastic knife, he cut the rope and lowered the monster. At the foot of the Tang Monk’s horse, the monster knelt with tear-filled eyes and did nothing but kowtow. The elder, being compassionate, called, “Child, climb onto my horse and I shall take you with us.” The monster replied, “Master, my hands and feet have gone numb from being tied up, and my waist and hips ache. Besides, I am a country child and am not accustomed to riding a horse.” The Tang Monk told Bajie to carry him. The monster glanced at him and said, “Master, my skin has been frozen tender, and I dare not ask this master to carry me. His snout is long, his ears are huge, and the bristles behind his head are stiff. I fear they will jab me.” The Tang Monk said, “Then let Friar Sand carry you.” The monster glanced at him too and said, “Master, when those bandits came to rob our house, every one of them had a painted face and a false beard and brandished knives and staves. They frightened me so badly that when I see this master’s ill-omened face, my soul flees me entirely. I dare not let him carry me either.” The Tang Monk told Sun Pilgrim to carry him. Pilgrim chuckled and said, “I will carry you. I will.” The monster rejoiced inwardly and readily agreed to let Pilgrim carry him.

p.src: Pilgrim pulled him to the roadside and tested his weight. He seemed to weigh only some three jin and ten-odd liang. Pilgrim laughed. “You wicked monster, your time to die has come today! How dare you play tricks before old Sun? I know you are one of those things.” The monster said, “I am a child of a respectable family who has had the misfortune to suffer this great calamity. How can I be any ‘such thing’?” Pilgrim said, “If you are a child of a respectable family, why are your bones so light?” The monster replied, “I have a small frame.” Pilgrim asked, “How old are you this year?” The monster replied, “I am seven.” Pilgrim laughed. “At one jin for every year, you should weigh seven jin. How is it you weigh less than four?” The monster said, “I lacked milk when I was little.” Pilgrim said, “Very well, then. I shall carry you, but if you need to piss or shit, you must tell me.”

p.src: As the Great Sage Sun carried the demon, he inwardly complained that the Tang Monk understood nothing of hardship: “Even unburdened, it is difficult to cross such steep mountain country, yet he makes old Sun carry someone. Never mind whether this wretch is a monster—even if he were a good person, with his parents gone, there is no telling to whom I should carry him. I might as well smash him to death.” The monster had already sensed his thoughts. He worked a spell, drew four breaths from the four directions, and blew them onto Pilgrim’s back, whereupon his weight seemed to become a thousand jin. Pilgrim laughed and said, “My child, you are using a weight-increasing spell to crush your old master.” Hearing this, the monster feared the Great Sage might injure him. He therefore abandoned his body, sent forth his primal spirit, leapt away, and stood high in the ninth heaven. The burden on Pilgrim’s back grew heavier still. Enraged, the Monkey King seized the body and, with a tremendous crash, hurled it onto a jagged rock beside the road, smashing the corpse flat as a meat cake. Still fearing it might cause more trouble, he tore off all four limbs and cast them on either side of the road, smashing them all to pieces.

p.src: The gale blew so fiercely that Tripitaka could scarcely remain in the saddle; Bajie dared not look up, while Sha Monk bowed his head and covered his face. The Great Sage Sun knew full well that a monster had raised the wind and hurried after it, but the creature had already ridden the gale away, carrying off the Tang Monk without trace or shadow. No one knew where it had taken him, and there was no trail to follow.

p.src: After a while the roar of the wind subsided, and the sunlight shone brightly again. Wukong went forward to look. The White Dragon Horse was trembling and neighing itself hoarse; the baggage lay abandoned beside the road; Bajie was groaning at the foot of a cliff; and Sha Monk crouched before the slope, calling out. Wukong called, “Bajie!” Hearing Wukong’s voice, the fool raised his head and saw that the violent wind had ceased. He scrambled up, seized Wukong, and said, “Brother, what a tremendous wind that was!” Sha Monk also came forward and said, “Brother, that was a whirlwind.” Then he asked, “Where is Master?” Bajie said, “The wind came so fiercely that we all ducked our heads, covered our eyes, and took shelter from it. Master was lying forward on his horse too.” Wukong said, “Then where has he gone now?” Sha Monk said, “He must be made of lampwick and have been swept away by a single gust.”

p.src: Wukong said, “Brothers, it seems we should part company here.” Bajie said, “Exactly. Let us separate while it is still early and each seek his own way. That would be far better. The road to the Western Heaven has no end in sight. When could we ever reach it?” Hearing this, Sha Monk started in alarm. His whole body went numb as he said, “Elder Brothers, what can you be saying? Because of sins in our former lives, we were blessed to receive the Bodhisattva Guanyin’s guidance. She touched our heads, gave us the precepts, changed our religious names, and set us on the path to Buddhahood. We willingly pledged to protect the Tang Monk on his journey west to worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures, redeeming our crimes through meritorious service. Now that we have come this far, how can we abandon everything at once and speak of each seeking his own road? Would that not betray the Bodhisattva’s benevolent purpose, ruin our own virtue, and make people mock us for beginning a task but never seeing it through?” Wukong said, “Brother, what you say is true. The trouble is that Master never listens to anyone. With my fiery eyes and golden pupils, I can tell good from evil. That wind just now was raised by the child who had been hanging from the tree. I knew he was a monster, though neither you nor Master recognized him. Master took him for the child of some decent family and ordered me to carry him. When I devised a plan to deal with him, he used a body-weight spell to crush me. So I dashed him to pieces. I suppose he used some body-shedding art, then raised a whirlwind and carried our master away. I am weary and disheartened because Master repeatedly refuses to listen to me. That is why I said we should all separate. Yet since you, worthy brother, possess such sincerity, you leave me unable either to advance or retreat. Bajie, what do you truly intend to do?” Bajie said, “I merely let my tongue run away with me and spoke a few wild words. In truth, we should not separate. Brother, there is nothing else for it. Let us heed Brother Sha, find that monster, and rescue Master.” Wukong’s anger turned to joy, and he said, “Brothers, let us unite our hearts once more, gather up the baggage and horse, climb the mountain to find the monster, and rescue Master.”

p.src: The three of them clung to creepers and pulled themselves along vines, searching slopes and circling ravines. After traveling some fifty or seventy li, they still found no trace or tidings. There were no birds or beasts anywhere on the mountain, only ancient cypresses and towering pines at every turn. The Great Sage Sun grew desperately anxious. With a single bound he leaped onto the summit of a steep and perilous peak and shouted, “Change!” He transformed himself into a being with three heads and six arms, just as he had appeared when wreaking havoc in Heaven. He shook the golden-hooped staff, changing it into three staffs, then, with a tremendous clatter and crash, beat a path eastward and another westward, striking wildly without cease on both sides. Seeing this, Bajie said, “Sha Monk, this is bad. Elder Brother cannot find Master, and frustration has driven him into a mad fit.”

p.src: After Wukong had thrashed about for a while, he beat out a whole band of wretched-looking gods. Each wore one rag and had another hanging from him; their loincloths lacked crotches and their trousers had no proper openings. Kneeling before the mountain, they cried, “Great Sage, the mountain gods and local earth gods have come to pay their respects.” Wukong said, “Why are there so many mountain gods and earth gods?” The gods knocked their heads against the ground and said, “We report to the Great Sage: this mountain is called the six-hundred-li Mount Numbered Drillhead. For every ten li there is one mountain god and one earth god, making thirty mountain gods and thirty earth gods in all. We heard yesterday that the Great Sage had arrived, but we could not assemble in time and were therefore late in welcoming you, causing the Great Sage to become angry. We humbly beg forgiveness.” Wukong said, “For now, I shall pardon your offense. Let me ask you: how many monsters live on this mountain?” The gods said, “Grandfather! There is only one monster, yet he has rubbed our heads bald and left us without incense, paper offerings, or sacrificial meat. Every one of us lacks clothes to cover his body and food to fill his mouth. How could we endure any more monsters?” Wukong said, “Does this monster live on the front of the mountain or the back?” The gods said, “He lives neither at the front nor at the back of the mountain. There is a ravine in this mountain called Withered Pine Ravine. Beside the ravine stands a cave called Fire-Cloud Cave. A demon king of vast magical powers lives inside. He often seizes us mountain gods and earth gods, makes us tend his fires and hold up the doors, and forces us to carry bells and call the watches for him through the night. His little fiends also demand their customary payments from us.” Wukong said, “You are spirits of the nether world who have attained divine rank. What money could you possess?” The gods said, “Precisely because we have no money to give them, we can only catch a few mountain roebucks and wild deer and use them morning and evening to satisfy the horde of fiends. If we have nothing to present, they come and tear down our temples, strip off our clothes, and torment us so badly that we cannot live in peace. We earnestly beg the Great Sage to exterminate this monster for us and save all the living creatures of the mountain.” Wukong said, “Since you are under his command and often attend his cave, do you know where this monster comes from and what he is called?” The gods said, “When we tell you who he is, perhaps the Great Sage will know of him. He is the son of the Bull Demon King, born and raised by the Rakshasa Woman. He cultivated his powers for three hundred years at the Mountain of Flames and mastered the True Fire of Samadhi. His magical powers are formidable, and the Bull Demon King sent him to guard Mount Numbered. His childhood name is Red Boy, and his title is the Great King Holy Infant.”

p.src: At these words, Monkey was delighted. He dismissed the local earth gods and mountain spirits, resumed his true form, and leapt down from the peak. Addressing Bajie and Friar Sand, he said, “Brothers, set your minds at ease and worry no more. Our master will certainly come to no harm, for that fiend is related to old Monkey.” Bajie laughed. “Brother, don’t tell lies. You are from the Eastern Continent of Superior Body, while this is the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift. The journey between them is long, across countless rivers and mountains and two great oceans besides. How could he be related to you?” Monkey said, “Those fellows just now were all the earth gods and mountain spirits of this region. When I asked them about the fiend’s origins, they told me he is the son of the Bull Demon King, born to the Rakshasi, and that his name is Red Boy and his title the Great King Holy Infant. Five hundred years ago, when old Monkey made havoc in Heaven, I roamed all the famous mountains under heaven in search of the heroes of the world, and the Bull Demon King and I became seven sworn brothers. Among those five or six demon kings, only old Monkey was small of stature, so I addressed the Bull Demon King as eldest brother. This fiend is the Bull Demon King’s son, and since I know his father, by the reckoning of kinship I am the boy’s old uncle. How would he dare harm my master? Let us go at once.” Friar Sand laughed. “Brother, as the saying goes, ‘After three years without a visit, even kin cease to be kin.’ You have been parted from him for five or six hundred years, without exchanging so much as a cup of wine or inviting each other to a single festival feast. Why should he acknowledge any kinship with you?” Monkey said, “Why do you judge others so narrowly? As the saying goes, ‘A drifting duckweed leaf returns to the great sea; wherever people go, they may meet again.’ Even if he refuses to acknowledge the kinship, surely he will not harm my master. I do not expect him to detain us for a banquet; he need only return the Tang Monk to me whole and sound.”

p.src: The three brothers each composed himself with sincere purpose, then set out straight along the main road, leading the white horse with the luggage loaded on its back. Traveling day and night, they covered somewhat over a hundred li before suddenly coming upon a pine forest. Through it wound a crooked ravine, along whose bottom clear living water rushed and sparkled. At the head of the ravine stood a stone-slab bridge leading to the cave dwelling on the other side. Monkey said, “Brothers, look at those jagged stone cliffs over there. That must be the fiend’s dwelling. Let us discuss this together: who will stay to guard the luggage and the horse? And who is willing to come with me to subdue the fiend?” Bajie said, “Brother, old Pig has no patience for sitting still. I’ll go with you.” “Good, good,” said Monkey. He instructed them, “Friar Sand, conceal the horse and luggage deep in the forest and guard them carefully, while the two of us go to the fiend’s door to seek our master.” Friar Sand obeyed. With Bajie following him, Monkey came forward, each of them bearing his weapon. And so it was that:
